# Incident Report: Network Forensic Analysis, MTA-2026-01-31

**Evidence:** `2026-01-31-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (51,181 packets, 27 MB, capture window 2026-01-28 03:04:03 to 03:14:27 UTC, ~624 sec). No supplementary IDS/Suricata exports were present in the evidence directory; findings are derived from the pcap alone via tshark.

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.1.21.58** |
| MAC address | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** (NetBIOS domain/workgroup: WIN11OFFICE, AD domain win11office.com) |
| Logged-in user | **gwyatt** (confirmed via Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString, realm WIN11OFFICE.COM, originating from 10.1.21.58) |

Confirmed via DHCP request (option 12 hostname "DESKTOP-ES9F3ML" for 10.1.21.58), NBNS name registration (workstation + WIN11OFFICE), and Kerberos traffic to the domain controller at 10.1.21.2 (MAC 14:b3:1f:2d:ce:69).

## 2. Malware Family

**Attribution: behavioral, not signature-confirmed.** No executable payload was transferred or captured in this pcap, and no hash/string in the traffic matches a publicly known malware signature I can independently verify without internet access. I am not naming a specific commodity family (e.g. a named stealer/RAT) because I have no PE, no config blob, and no confirmed signature to back that claim.

What the traffic does show, concretely:
- A JavaScript-driven **browser fingerprinting-and-check-in beacon** served from `whitepepper.su` (153.92.1.49) collecting `navigator`, WebGL, and canvas fingerprint data and POSTing it back to a `/api/set_agent` panel, tagged with a victim GUID/token pair.
- The beacon executed twice ~8 seconds apart, once tagged `agent=Chrome` and once `agent=Edge` (identical script apart from that parameter), consistent with an automated check of both installed browsers.
- Following the two fingerprint check-ins, the host opened **18 short-lived TLS connections to the same C2 IP (153.92.1.49:443)** between t=92s and t=122s, several carrying large, rapid **outbound-heavy** bursts (e.g. 1.4 MB sent by the victim in 2.8 seconds; 404 KB in 2.2 seconds; 263 KB in 1.8 seconds) — a traffic shape consistent with automated exfiltration of harvested data, though content is TLS-encrypted and cannot be inspected.
- This was preceded by DNS resolutions to several suspicious-looking domains (fake file-hosting-style names, uncommon TLDs) in the ~45–126 second window, suggesting a redirect/gate chain leading into the whitepepper.su check-in, though those sessions are also TLS/QUIC-encrypted and no plaintext payload could be recovered from them.

Functional characterization: a **browser-fingerprinting C2 / stealer check-in and exfiltration beacon**, most consistent in behavior with a fake-verification ("ClickFix"-style) delivery/tracking gate. Treat the specific family name as unconfirmed until the host or full-content capture is available for static/dynamic analysis.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise (grounded in observed traffic)

**Confirmed C2 (cleartext HTTP, directly observed request/response):**
- `whitepepper.su` — 153.92.1.49:80 (fingerprint logging) and 153.92.1.49:443 (TLS, high-volume outbound bursts, likely exfil channel)

**Malicious/suspicious URLs (verbatim from capture):**
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log` (POST, fingerprint data)
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge&act=log` (POST, fingerprint data)

**Victim tracking ID (unique identifiers seen in the panel URLs):**
- id: `3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C`
- token: `842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b`

**Transferred files and hashes (JS/HTML fingerprinting payloads pulled from the exported HTTP objects, SHA256):**
- Chrome-tagged fingerprint script (`set_agent?...agent=Chrome`): `a1ee2e3055dc4ce0d60eb6c2c8a655e705b3607bd33d65794e67adf22a2a0124`
- Edge-tagged fingerprint script (`set_agent?...agent=Edge`): `8f97a4018d4b0675b9592660394cf5b73f1be2252e27aff64a8f160af9079f46`
- `favicon.ico` served by whitepepper.su: `74ab801591b951bcb6b248a8ef9321388a45ecf8badd2893aea4aa360b26ea90`

No downloaded executable (.exe/.dll) was present in the HTTP object stream — the only reconstructable transfers are the two near-identical JS fingerprint pages and the favicon above.

**Suspicious domains resolved shortly before the C2 check-in (encrypted TLS/QUIC sessions, content unverifiable, listed for pivoting/blocking):**
| Domain | Resolved IP | First seen (t, sec) |
|---|---|---|
| hiyter.com | — | 45.3 |
| media.megafilehub4.lat | 104.21.48.156 | 45.8 |
| arch.filemegahab4.sbs | — | 48.3 |
| whooptm.cyou | 62.72.32.156 | 90.3 |
| whitepepper.su | 153.92.1.49 | 92.3 |
| holiday-forever.cc | 80.97.160.24 | 122.8 |
| communicationfirewall-security.cc | 104.21.9.36 | 126.5 |

These domains are flagged as suspicious by naming pattern (fake file-hosting/cloaking-style names on uncommon TLDs) and by their temporal proximity to the confirmed C2 beacon; recommend blocking/sinkholing pending deeper review, but their role in the infection chain is not independently confirmed from this pcap alone since their sessions are encrypted.

## Recommended Actions
1. Isolate 10.1.21.58 (DESKTOP-ES9F3ML) from the network immediately.
2. Block outbound traffic to 153.92.1.49 (whitepepper.su) and the six domains/IPs listed above at the perimeter/DNS layer.
3. Perform host-based forensics (disk/memory acquisition) on DESKTOP-ES9F3ML to recover the dropper/executable and any browser extension or scheduled task responsible for driving the fingerprinting requests — this pcap alone cannot yield a confirmed malware family name.
4. Reset credentials for user `gwyatt` given the large outbound TLS bursts to the C2, which are consistent with credential/data exfiltration.
